verdicts.trueWording: Martin's evocative storytelling style and gift for gripping narrative are mostly absent from this dry history
verdicts.note: Live publishersweekly.com page, review dated 11/19/2018: opening sentence reads verbatim 'Martin's evocative storytelling style and gift for gripping narrative are mostly absent from this dry history of the blood-drenched Targaryens'. Quote and every limb (2018, PW, Fire & Blood) confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin gives equal weight to each member of the Targaryen family
verdicts.note: Same PW page: '...concluding with the ascent of young King Aegon III..., Martin gives equal weight to each member of the Targaryen family.' Quote verbatim; the claim's 'each member of the Targaryen family' is the page's own wording.

verdicts.trueWording: there are entertaining snatches of dialogue and detailed depictions of battles
verdicts.note: Same PW page: 'Brief sections are dramatic (...) or salacious (...), and there are entertaining snatches of dialogue and detailed depictions of battles, but they only last a few pages before a return to brisk summary.' Quote verbatim and the 'brief dramatic sections' limb is the same sentence's subject. The review's qualifier (they last only a few pages) is omitted by the claim but not contradicted.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin aficionados are used to eldritch epochal terms such as the Doom of Valyria
verdicts.note: Live kirkusreviews.com page, ld+json reviewBody first sentence: 'Martin aficionados are used to eldritch epochal terms such as the Doom of Valyria and the Dance of the Dragons...'. Quote verbatim. Page metadata confirms 'Review Posted Online: Jan. 20, 2019', so the 2019 limb holds. Wording note: the review says 'Martin aficionados', not 'Martin's readers' - a faithful but slightly broadened paraphrase; quote the source as 'aficionados'.

verdicts.trueWording: rather than abandoning or subverting the conventions of his genre, is actually using them particularly well
verdicts.note: Live journal.finfar.org page: 'he argues that Martin, rather than "abandoning or subverting the conventions of his genre, is actually using them particularly well" (5)'. Quote verbatim, Young's page 5 cited on the page, review signed C. Palmer-Patel, Fafnir vol. 9 iss. 1 pp. 117-121, page metadata rft.date=2022-06-29.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin tends to use a low mimetic register in both his characters and descriptions
verdicts.note: Higgins PDF (Wayback raw capture of scholar.valpo.edu viewcontent, 7-page PDF, text extracted): 'In the first chapter "The American Pratchett-Muck and Modality," Young explores how Martin tends to use a "low mimetic" register in both his characters and descriptions to bring his fantasy closer to reality.' Quote verbatim; Chapter 1 attribution confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: the literary iceberg in which stories are strengthened by leaving things or events out
verdicts.note: Same Higgins PDF: 'Honegger explores Ernest Hemingway's concept in his essay "The Art of the Short Story" (1959) of the "literary iceberg" in which stories are strengthened by leaving things or events out.' Quote verbatim; applied to Martin two sentences later ('with Tolkien and Martin we are dealing with two very different icebergs' / Martin's 'literary iceberg').

verdicts.trueWording: invented his world from the top down ... with the backstories being invented after the main narratives
verdicts.note: Same Higgins PDF: 'Martin started writing A Song of Ice and Fire in the 1990's and invented his world from the top down-his "literary iceberg" was invented coterminous with the stories, with the backstories being invented after the main narratives.' Quote verbatim; sits inside the Honegger chapter discussion, so the Honegger attribution holds.

verdicts.trueWording: I, alas, am only a hardworking SF and Fantasy novel[ist] and I don't have a gift for languages
verdicts.note: Same Higgins PDF: 'Martin was quite clear as he said in an interview that Honegger cites, "Tolkien was a philologist... I, alas, am only a hardworking SF and Fantasy novel[ist] and I don't have a gift for languages" (159).' Quote verbatim, negation correctly reported, Honegger p.159 citation present on the page.

Walsworth digital edition of Math Horizons, April 2016, section 'The Social Network': 'The 107 vertices represent the characters, including ladies and lords, guards and mercenaries...' followed by 'We generated the edges using A Storm of Swords, the third book in the series.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The King's Landing community accounts for 37 percent of the network
verdicts.note: Same article, Community Detection: 'In our case, we discover the seven communities in figure 2. The King's Landing community accounts for 37 percent of the network.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: The network layout and colors in figure 2 clearly identify seven communities
verdicts.note: Same article, Community Detection opening: 'The network layout and colors in figure 2 clearly identify seven communities: the Lannisters and King's Landing, Robb's army, Bran and friends, Arya and companions, Jon Snow and the far North, Stannis's forces, and Daerenys and the exotic people of Essos.' Quote verbatim; the network is the A Storm of Swords one.

verdicts.trueWording: This is the only measure in which Tyrion does not come out on top
verdicts.note: Same article, Centrality Measures: 'Betweenness centrality gives a distinctive ranking of the characters. This is the only measure in which Tyrion does not come out on top: He places third, behind Jon Snow ... and Robert Baratheon...'. Quote verbatim; the measure named is betweenness, as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: From the five books containing 343 chapters, 2,007 characters were identified, of which 1,806 interact with another at least once
verdicts.note: PNAS live URL returned HTTP 403; recovered via Wayback raw capture (web.archive.org/web/20250710185328id_/) - full publisher text, dc.Date 2020-11-17. Results, 'Evolution of the Social Network Structure': the sentence appears verbatim. Total identified is 2,007; 1,806 is the interacting subset, as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: the number of characters per chapter settles at around 35
verdicts.note: Same PNAS Wayback raw capture: 'After a short period of growth in the first book, in which the main characters are introduced, the number of characters per chapter settles at around 35.' Quote verbatim. The paper locates the growth period inside the first book and Fig. 2 caption says it 'fluctuates around 35 by the end of A Game of Thrones', which supports the claim's 'after the opening book'.
